Howard Hughes. The aviation pioneer and industrialist whose reckless flying style, engineering ambition, and later eccentricity made him one of aviation's most polarizing figures. In 1935, Hughes set a world air-speed record of three hundred fifty-two miles per hour, flying his custom Hughes H-1 Racer. Three years later, he flew around the world in a twin-engine Lockheed fourteen, completing the journey in three days and nineteen hours. Hughes founded Hughes Aircraft Company, which became a major defense contractor and manufacturer. He owned and ran Trans World Airlines, or TWA, transforming it into a major transatlantic airline before selling his stake in nineteen sixty-six. His most ambitious design was the Hughes H-4 Hercules, an enormous flying boat that was the largest aircraft ever built. Despite suffering injuries in several crashes, Hughes continued to personally fly experimental aircraft. In his later years, he withdrew from public life, becoming increasingly reclusive and eccentric as his wealth and isolation fueled legend. His experimental aircraft ambitions paralleled those of Chuck Yeager, though Yeager pursued supersonic flight while Hughes pursued other records. He shared his era with speed-setter Wiley Post and pioneering aviator Jimmy Doolittle.
